claim: On RustFS, four minutes into a soak, enumeration of a ref-log stream returned `seq 0x1430e` while omitting predecessors `0x1430c` and `0x1430d`.
The omitted ref-log objects `0x1430c` and `0x1430d` had been durable for approximately 19 seconds before the anomaly fired.
At the moment of the RustFS LIST disagreement, an exact-key `HEAD` confirmed that each omitted object was present.
Across 65,263 ref-log uploads in the affected namespace, partitioned by epoch, zero uploads were out of order.
The RustFS incident investigation excluded concurrent deletion as an explanation for the omitted ref-log objects.
The RustFS incident investigation excluded stale-epoch minting as an explanation for the omitted ref-log objects.
The RustFS incident investigation excluded out-of-order appends as an explanation for the omitted ref-log objects.
The RustFS incident investigation excluded a late `Unresolved` PUT as an explanation for the omitted ref-log objects.
The RustFS incident had a correct LIST tail; its lie was omission of predecessors below the returned frontier rather than tail under-reporting.
On contract-compliant S3, omission of predecessors below a correct LIST tail is legal when writes are concurrent with a paginated enumeration.
S3 read-after-write consistency for LIST covers enumerations started after a PUT completes, but does not provide a snapshot contract for keys that land during an existing paginated walk.
During a paginated S3 walk, a key landing behind the pagination marker can be invisible while a later key ahead of the marker is visible.
The observed RustFS omission was a contract violation under AWS-style semantics because the omitted keys were durable approximately 19 seconds before the enumeration began.
Tail under-reporting of a completed write is illegal on a compliant S3 store because it violates the read-after-write clause.
A per-backend trust mode may rely only on the compliant-S3 property that LIST cannot under-report the tail of a completed write.
No LIST violation of any kind has been observed on AWS S3; the incident is evidence about RustFS and about concurrency permitted during enumeration, not about AWS S3.
During the RustFS incident, exact-key `GET` and `HEAD` returned the truth while LIST omitted objects that were present.
Conditional writes are trusted as fences because a store cannot return `Created` for `putIfAbsent` on an existing key without destroying its own data.
The CAS trust chain is catalog cut for the universe, `_ckpt` for the acknowledged frontier, exact `GET`s for records, and conditional writes for fences.
LIST is treated as a hint for work bounds, witness sets, and genesis discovery; a LIST lie in either direction may delay reclamation but must never authorize destruction.

A stale-but-honest read represents a true cut from the past, so its errors tend toward retention or delay and are closed forward by the round-paced floor, exact-token delete, delete-site in-degree re-read, and `Gc/CasBlobInDegree.cpp` temporal arms.
A fabricated cut created by omission under a seal corresponds to no point in time; folding it and sealing above hidden records can authorize destruction and is unrecoverable.
Delay-shaped errors are acceptable in CAS reclamation, but authorization-shaped errors are not.
Three hammer runs listing approximately 19 million keys produced zero holes before a LIST violation occurred live within four minutes of an ordinary RustFS soak.
A mount-time synthetic probe that PUTs a few keys, LISTs them, and compares the result cannot certify a backend, because it will pass on virtually every store, including RustFS.
A bucket passport may be based on operator attestation that the bucket is an AWS or GCS bucket with documented strong LIST semantics.
The LIST trust mode is a runtime property of an individual bucket, never a property of a backend type string.

A bucket may retain trust only with continuous verification and auto-revocation: background exact-key probes or `_ckpt`-versus-tail cross-checks must run, and the first observed lie must permanently demote the bucket to probe-always while recording an anomaly.
Sampling bounds detection time but not exposure of unsampled namespaces during the detection window, so continuous verification is a risk-acceptance knob rather than proof of backend correctness.
The combined passport policy is attestation to enable trust plus verification to revoke it, with probe-always as the fail-close default whenever there is doubt.
RustFS fails the bucket-passport requirement based on the measured LIST violation.
Arithmetic middle intake is mandatory on every backend, because predecessor omission below a correct tail is legal during concurrent enumeration.
Frontier probes remain required for held namespaces and for namespaces with no listed logs.
The condition `tail < cursor` continues to feed the store-quality detector.
The only backend-gradeable LIST claim is that `tail == cursor` proves the frontier, and this may be used only under a bucket passport with the settled attestation and verification properties.
The parallel-walk optimization is trust-neutral and requires no LIST-trust passport.
